newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rebels throw big party for N.Korean crew.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rebels throw big party for N.Korean crew.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Tamil Tiger rebels organised a farewell party for the crew of a North Korean ship they siezed earlier this week before releasing them, a Red Cross official said on Saturday.

Sivanathan Kishore, northeast coordinator for the Sri Lanka Red Cross, who went into the northern rebel-held Wanni region to secure the crew's release, told Reuters the rebels sang songs and played instruments at the party late on Friday.

"They (the rebels) were in their uniforms. They also asked the North Koreans to sing. The party lasted two hours," Kishore said over phone from government-held town of Vavuniya, some 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo.
He said the crew of the seized ship had been brought to Vavuniya and were on their way to Colombo by road.

A spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross earlier said the 37 surviving crew of the Morang Bong, seized by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) late on Monday, would be handed over to the ship's agent in Colombo.
He said officials from the North Korean embassy in New Delhi had arrived in Colombo on Saturday to recieve the crew. The Stalinist nation does not have diplomatic presence in Sri Lanka.
The body of the ship's fourth officer, killed in a shootout as the rebels took control of the ship off the northern Jaffna peninsula, was handed over to the ICRC on Wednesday.
An official of the ship's agent, Monsell International, said on Wednesday the Morang Bong had just unloaded nearly 3,000 tonnes of food and other supplies in Point Pedro when it was hijacked.
The rebels, who are fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east, said they had seized the ship because "it was sailing within Tamil Eelam's territorial waters".
Last Tuesday a Defence Ministry statement said the ship had been "chartered by traders from Colombo to carry essential goods to Point Pedro... for the civilians in the north".
Rebels have cut the strategic highway connecting the peninsula with the rest of Sri Lanka so food and other essentials must be taken in by sea or air.

In an earlier incident, the rebels last week set fire to a refugee ship off the northwestern coast and took away its nine crew, including two Indonesians who were later released. The fate of the remaining seven Sri Lankan crew is unknown.
The two incidents have led to cancellation of most shipping services to the north. Government officials in Vavuniya said shipping lines were demanding naval escort before resuming services.

Sri Lankan troops launched a big offensive against the rebels in May in an attempt to reopen the highway, but the operation slowed in June after the LTTE launched two fierce counterattacks. Scores of soldiers and rebels were killed.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
